##### **Executive Summary**

This deliverable of WP2 describes the 6GARROW architecture approach by determining a common methodology and process for evolving and updating the initial architecture in the subsequent tasks and phases of the project. To establish a solid starting point to the design of the architectural, techno-economic aspects of AI-native architecture are examined in detail. A balanced approach that acknowledges both the transformative potential of AI integration and the practical challenges of implementation is needed. Rapid advances in AI technology create risks of premature obsolescence for network investments, necessitating flexible architecture design and upgrade paths to protect long-term investments. The state-of-the-art analysis covers relevant standardization; 3GPP being the primary one supported by ETSI, O-RAN and several industry initiatives. activities and research initiatives. AI-native 6G network architectures have been researched by some project under the Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking umbrella. A summary of current architectural considerations is provided. Based on D2.1, "6GARROW Scenarios, Use Cases and related KPIs/KVIs," a gap analysis is carried out to identify missing and new functionality. Building on this, we propose an initial functional architecture that supports a semantic layer and common AI orchestration for task-specific semantic operations. We extend the current QoS indicators to include predictive QoS that is needed by AI agents to anticipate future traffic needs. ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) 6GARROW Deliverable D2.2

##### **1 Introduction**

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) models have been leveraged by network operators and vendors already for some time, primarily as implementation choice to augment established conventional methodologies in domains such as network operations administration and management (OAM). In this initial phase of adoption, AI/ML functions in an assistive capacity, acting as an optimization agent that facilitates the selection and refinement of operational parameters within pre-existing, classical network functions in limited contexts. This role represents an algorithmic refinement or software overlay that preserves the fundamental architecture while yielding incremental efficiency gains. Conversely, within the architectural context of 6G networks, AI/ML is taken as a fundamentally transformative paradigm. This shift entails the replacement of classical network functions with AI/ML-powered counterparts, whose operational design is intrinsically optimized for and dependent on machine intelligence. It involves substituting static, deterministic logic with learned policies or data-driven models, thereby enabling performance gains (e.g., in latency or energy efficiency) that are unattainable through mere network function reconfiguration by OAM and orchestrator systems. Moving beyond network function-level adoption of AI/ML – feasible in 5G network functions as an isolated deployment – the ultimate goal is the comprehensive deployment of AI/ML across multiple network functions and subsystems. This systemic integration leads to the realization of an AI-native architecture. By extending AI governance over interconnected chains of network functions, a holistic, system-level approach can be achieved, focusing on efficient cross-function and cross-system data exposure and AI model sharing. 6G will build its capabilities on distributed cloud infrastructures, enabling flexible resource allocation and dynamic orchestration – a prerequisite for supporting AI-native workloads. The most challenging task in defining the AI-native architecture the seamless integration of AI/ML into the existing layered architecture of current networks, along with the corresponding enhancements to protocol stacks. It is expected that 6G wireless standards will incorporate AI-native functionalities and design principles as next-generation network architectures and their component are defined. Overall, the integration of AI/ML into 6G will fundamentally transform how networks are specified, designed, and implemented. **1.1 Objective of this deliverable** The objective of this deliverable is to establish a solid common understanding of the AI native architecture within the 6GARROW project. To accomplish this, we analyse state-of-the-art proposals from key Standard Developing Organizations (SDOs), industry initiatives and research projects. Based on this analysis, a gap analysis is conducted to identify missing functionalities expected to be required for implementing the use case families and use cases defined in D2.1. To ensure the architectural framework remains economically relevant, techno-economic aspects are considered alongside the Key Performance Indicator (KPI)/KVS defined in D2.1 [6GARROW-D21]. Furthermore, the adopted methodology ensures that the proposed architecture does not omit any critical aspects supported by other architectures referenced in the SNS-JU White Paper [SNS2025Arch]. **1.2 Structure of the document** Chapter 2 describes the design methodology and underlying principles, while Chapter 3 addresses the techno-economic aspects that lead to recommendations for the incremental introduction of the proposed architecture. Chapter 4 presents a state-of-the-art survey and analysis covering key SDOs and relevant research projects. ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) 6GARROW Deliverable D2.2 Chapter 5 provides a use-case-driven gap analysis that serves as the basis for drafting the initial architecture. This is followed by an examination of core and radio network enhancements required to integrate AI-native functionality into a jointly optimized RAN–CN architectural view. Section 5.4 documents the proposed architecture, which will be further refined in Deliverable D2.4 (M30) based on findings from Work Packages 3, 4, and 5.

##### **2 Methodology and principle**

This chapter sets out the methodology used to outline and design the 6GARROW architecture from the project drivers defined in D2.1 and relevant standards baselines. It begins by establishing foundations, i.e. assumptions, constraints, and explicit inputs such as scenarios, use cases, and KPIs/KVIs. It then specifies how a gap analysis against the state of the art will identify missing capabilities and design pressures. Based on these deltas, the chapter sets out how candidate design options are to be generated and compared using explicit selection criteria and trade-offs, and how subsequent evaluation should be conducted (e.g., trace-driven simulations, digital twins, PoC testbeds) against quantitative KPI/KVI thresholds, including proxy metrics where AI-nativeness lacks direct benchmarks. Figure 1 summarizes this closed loop; the architectural choices and their evaluations are developed in later chapters. **Figure 1. 6GARROW architecture design flowchart with respect to the WPs: assumptions and constraints feed a gap analysis grounded in D2.1 scenarios/use cases and KPIs/KVIs; results are** **evaluated against target thresholds, with failures looping back to refine assumptions and successes concluding the design.** **2.1 Foundations of the design methodology** To establish guiding principles for architecture development, we adopt ITU-T Recommendation Y.2012 [ITU12] which specifies the functional requirements and architecture of a Next Generation Network (NGN). This Recommendation defines functional entities (FEs) of different scopes. The FEs are grouped into different stratums: services and transport stratums. Stratums and FEs are used for identifying and defining reference points and information flows across subsystems. Combining these ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) 6GARROW Deliverable D2.2 principles with the current system architecture for the 5G System (5GS) [TS23.501] we adopt the following guidelines:

  * The architecture shall be service-oriented,
  * The architecture should integrate different access technologies (fixed, mobile, wireless, etc.),
  * The architecture supports the following o different Quality of Service (QoS) levels, o openness, interoperability, and Application Programming Interface (API) exposure, o separation of control and user planes, o sustainability and energy consumption awareness, o trustworthiness, persistent security, and privacy by design, o AI/ML-enabled automation and optimization, o scalability, resilience, and smooth migration from 5G standalone architecture. SNS-JU White Paper [SNS2025Arch] provides a list of architecture design principles and their impact on 6G E2E system design.
